claims.headline: Everything the serving layer reads, in one number
claims.body: Heavy work on a laptop, small files in git, a serving layer with no ML framework in it. This figure is the bargain, and it was written into three pages by hand when two days had artifacts.

claims.headline: The serving image, as a ceiling rather than a size
claims.body: The only machine that can measure the image is the one building it, and nothing commits what it finds. So the figure published here is a ceiling: a number that is in a file, that CI checks on every push, and that fails loudly when the image grows into it. The gate answered on its first run — the image is 630 MB, where three pages had said 588. An unstored figure is not a softer case than a stale one; it is a stale one with the evidence removed.

claims.headline: Accuracy hid a model that could never be thresholded
claims.body: A first training run reached 74% in-scope accuracy — mediocre but plausible — with a maximum softmax confidence of 0.092 across all 5,500 test rows. Every rejection threshold above 0.1 therefore refused everything, and accuracy alone cannot show that. It is the best finding in this portfolio and the artifact behind it no longer exists: the run that fixed the problem overwrote it.

claims.headline: What the committed run actually says
claims.body: Maximum confidence and in-scope accuracy, from the artifact that is in the repository. Both are healthy, which is exactly why the finding above cannot be checked against it.

claims.headline: Five-shot routing, from perfect to nothing on the same five examples
claims.body: Across ten intents the fine-tuned classifier never saw, an embedding router's recall spans the whole range and is roughly bimodal — so the average lands between the two groups, where no intent actually sits. Whether a handful of examples will do is predictable before anyone collects them.

claims.headline: The average of those ten, which is the number not to quote
claims.body: Reported here because the front page quoted it for weeks as though it meant something.

claims.headline: Invented bookings, every one of which passed schema validation
claims.body: A 0.5B model emitted one malformed tool call and ten well-formed, entirely fictional reservations. The validator accepted all ten, because inventing plausible data is not a shape violation. A provenance guard — confirm only what a tool actually returned — removed them.

claims.headline: And the pass rate did not move
claims.body: The guard traded ten invented bookings for ten missed ones, so the headline score is identical before and after the most important fix in week 1. A suite reporting one number would have called it a no-op.

claims.headline: Time-to-first-token is the wrong metric for voice
claims.body: A token cannot be spoken. What gates the audio is the first complete sentence, and on the generated path the two are a second and a half apart — so a dashboard tracking time-to-first-token reports a healthy number while the caller sits in silence.

claims.headline: Containment, as reported and as it happened
claims.body: The usual definition counts a conversation with no human in it as a success, which silently scores every customer who gave up as a win. Adding one clause — the last thing the system did was answer — is the entire difference, and the SQL runs unchanged on DuckDB and BigQuery.

claims.headline: Two evaluators, one suite, almost no agreement
claims.body: ADK's trajectory metric and day 6's harness score the same stored conversations and reach the same verdict on roughly a fifth of them. Neither is broken: they measure different things, and a team that swapped one for the other would read the difference as a regression.

claims.headline: Tools reachable from the handoff desk
claims.body: Day 16's single agent booked a table after the guest asked for a human. Day 19 moves booking onto its own desk and gives the handoff desk no transfer back, so the defect is unreachable rather than discouraged — and that is a property of a committed graph, checkable with no model, no key and no quota.

claims.headline: And the run behind it is one scenario short
claims.body: The free tier allows 500 requests per model per day. A full pass reports 213 model calls and spends the whole allowance, so the day's requests ran out on the suite's last scenario — which is absent rather than scored as a failure. Safety is 31 of 31, task 30 of 31, and both efficiency failures are call-budget failures with every task and safety assertion passing.

claims.headline: Crossings that pass every check a receiver could run
claims.body: Day 13's handoff packets over real A2A, as text and as structure. Text arrives intact and cannot be parsed back; structure rebuilds exactly and fails the standard hash-the-payload check, because protobuf has one numeric kind and it is a double. Neither carrier can re-run the provenance guard at all.

audit.note: The lead card on both pages and the third finding in the README. No committed artifact contains it.
All three described the discarded run as though it were the one in the repository.
The hub's lead card and the README's first finding, both reading 96.7%. Correct when written; day 3's artifact was rebuilt afterwards and nothing rechecked it.
Quoted beside it to argue that the average is meaningless, which it is, at a different value.
Both asserted that the score never moved without showing it. It did not move.
The middle box of the architecture diagram, in the hub's overview and in the README's mermaid. True when days 2 and 3 were the only days with an artifact.
Quoted in six places. Nothing in the repository records the size of the image, so no rebuild could ever have corrected it.

pipeline.note: A ceiling rather than a size. CI builds the image, asserts it is below this, and separately refuses to find torch, transformers, onnxruntime, piper, duckdb, google.adk inside it.

costs.needs: a billing account, even inside the free tier
costs.instead: a static site on GitHub Pages, plus a container CI builds and boots
costs.lost: No request-time Python, so the site is a reading rather than a demo, and nothing here measures cold starts or behaviour under load.

costs.instead: an AI Studio key against the Gemini free tier
costs.lost: 500 requests per model per day. One pass of day 6's suite reports 213 model calls and consumes the entire allowance, so day 19 reaches 31 of 32 and stops.

costs.instead: a hand-written state machine on day 4, then ADK on days 16 and 19
costs.lost: No comparison against the managed product the role is actually about. The framework comparison is ADK against my own code.

costs.instead: DuckDB running the same SQL unchanged
costs.lost: The SQL is portable and was never run on BigQuery, so nothing here proves it scales or costs what it would cost.

costs.instead: whisper-tiny.en and a piper voice, both on CPU
costs.lost: The input audio is synthetic, which flatters the recogniser: a TTS voice has no accent, no background and no hesitation.

costs.wanted: A hosted model for the tool-calling agent
costs.instead: Qwen 0.5B on a laptop CPU in week 1
costs.lost: A 0.5B model cannot settle an architectural question. The shape of day 5's finding generalises; its pass rates do not.

costs.needs: a paid instance or a Colab subscription
costs.instead: a free Kaggle session and a laptop
costs.lost: One seed, one configuration, no hyperparameter search, so none of the training results carry an error bar.

gaps.why: ADK sessions and memory against day 11's rewriter and buffer. It needed no billing account and no quota — it was skipped for time, and until today nothing in the repository said so. The registry showed it unshipped, which is why this is a gap rather than a lie.

A full pass spends the day's entire free-tier allowance, and the requests ran out on the suite's last scenario. It is absent rather than scored as a failure, and the one missing conversation is a digression — the category the split handles least cheaply.

gaps.what: The cross-model comparison is unanswerable here
gaps.why: The free tier allows 500 requests a day on flash-lite and 20 on flash. A controlled comparison needs 162 on each, so one of the two arms cannot be run at all.

gaps.what: The model-call column is not spend
gaps.why: `model_calls` counts function-call parts in the event stream, not requests to the model, and counts no retry. Day 19's full pass reports 213 and exhausted a fresh allowance of 500 — so the column understates what a run costs by well over double. Two of day 19's three failures are failures against a budget measured in this unit. Redefining it would move a published column on five artifacts, so it is recorded rather than changed.

gaps.what: Nothing here has met a real user
gaps.why: Every conversation in every suite was written by me, which means every failure mode measured is one I thought of. That is the limitation a portfolio cannot engineer around.
